justice: The route is an unpaved dirt-and-gravel track rather than a formal street space, so transport infrastructure is not equitably provided for different users.
There is no visible sidewalk, curb separation, or marked pedestrian zone, meaning walking space is not fairly allocated relative to the vehicle track.
Accessibility is weak because the surface is uneven with potholes, loose stones, and edge drop-offs that hinder strollers, wheelchairs, and people with limited mobility.
No curb ramps, tactile paving, or formal crossing facilities are visible, indicating limited barrier-free design for a broad range of users.
safety: The roadway surface is broken and irregular, with potholes and gravel that increase slipping, tripping, and vehicle instability risks.
The road edge near the lakeside appears informal and undefined, creating potential runoff or fall hazards for pedestrians and cyclists.
Construction-related vehicles and materials ahead, including trucks and piles of aggregate, introduce conflict points and reduce predictability of movement.
There are no visible lane markings, traffic signs, guardrails, or lighting devices to organize movement or improve user safety.
livability: The setting is isolated and lacks visible shops, services, seating, or active frontages that would support daily social and practical use.
The road appears to function mainly as an access track near a development area rather than a complete public street for community life.
The lakeside and open sky provide some recreational and visual value, but the absence of amenities limits everyday livability.
Sparse human activity and unfinished surroundings reduce the sense of neighborhood vitality and convenience.
sustainability: The presence of trees, shrubs, and a large water body contributes ecological value and some landscape permeability.
The largely unsealed ground around the track may allow rainwater infiltration better than fully paved surfaces.
However, the environment is strongly car- and construction-access oriented, with no visible public transport stop or dedicated active-mobility infrastructure.
Young trees are present but canopy cover is still limited, so current cooling, carbon, and habitat benefits remain modest.
aesthetics: The waterfront view and expansive sky create a visually open and pleasant natural backdrop.
Greenery along both sides of the track softens the scene and adds some landscape interest.
At the same time, the rough dirt road, scattered stones, and construction-related vehicles reduce visual refinement.
High-rise buildings under construction in the distance make the area feel unfinished rather than cohesively designed.
comfort: Thermal comfort is limited because the young trees provide very little continuous shade along the route.
Physical comfort is poor due to the uneven dirt-and-gravel surface with bumps, potholes, and loose material underfoot or under wheels.
There are no benches, shelters, or resting facilities visible, reducing comfort for anyone spending time outdoors here.
Psychological comfort is weakened by the isolated setting, unfinished development context, and lack of clearly protected space for non-motorized users.
walkability: There is no dedicated sidewalk or clearly defined pedestrian path, so walking must occur on the same rough access road used by vehicles.
The walking surface is discontinuous and uncomfortable because of gravel, patched dirt, potholes, and irregular edges.
No crosswalks, curb ramps, signage, lighting, or wayfinding elements are visible to support pedestrian movement.
Limited shade and no seating make longer walks less attractive and less accommodating for a wide range of users.
bikeability: There is no bike lane, shoulder, or marked cycling space, forcing cyclists to share an uneven access track with vehicles.
The loose gravel, potholes, and broken surface would make cycling unstable and uncomfortable, especially for casual riders.
Construction vehicles and roadside materials ahead increase conflict risk and reduce perceived cycling safety.
No bicycle parking, lane markings, or intersection treatments are visible to support cycling as a regular mode.
